t: Most Frequent IDs — Hash Map + Lazy Heap
o: Simulate additions/removals with a frequency map, and after each step report the maximum frequency. A plain max-heap goes stale because frequencies decrease on removals. Trick: push a new entry `(freq, id)` every time an id's frequency changes, and pop heap tops whose recorded frequency no longer matches the map. n ≤ 1e5, so O(n log n) is ideal.
k: Lazy deletion: a heap entry is valid iff its freq equals the map's current freq for that id.

a.i: Update the map, push the new (freq,id) pair, then discard stale tops before reading the max.
s: While top's stored freq ≠ map value, pop.
a.t: O(n log n) — each step pushes once; amortized pops bounded by pushes

a.i: Keep a multiset (sorted container) of all current frequencies alongside the map. On each update, erase the old frequency and insert the new one; the answer is the multiset's maximum. Deterministic O(log n) per step without lazy cleanup.
s: Maintain map id→freq and multiset of frequencies.
On update: remove old freq from multiset, add new freq.
Answer = largest element of the multiset (0 if empty).

w: Frequencies fit in 64-bit (up to 1e10 cumulative), so use long types. The lazy heap is the idiomatic interview answer; mention the ordered-set alternative. Follow-up: segment tree over frequencies compressed by coordinate also works.
